patient_information: A 67-year-old German woman, who has lived as an expatriate in Cameroon for the past 4 years. Her past medical history is otherwise unremarkable.
chief_complaint: Palpitations and transient subcutaneous swellings for the past year.
history_of_present_illness: A 67-year-old German woman presents with palpitations at a tropical medicine clinic in Germany, and also reports transient subcutaneous swellings for the past year. There is no history of fever or constitutional symptoms. A 24-hour ECG recording done elsewhere showed paroxysmal supraventricular extrasystoles. Echocardiography revealed a minimal pericardial effusion.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient has lived as an expatriate in Cameroon for the past 4 years.
vitals: Vital signs are normal and the patient is afebrile.
physical_exam: There are no visible subcutaneous swellings. Heart sounds are clear and regular, and there are no murmurs. No pathological findings are noted on physical examination.
labs_and_diagnostics: Full blood count results show WBC 6.20 (×10^9/L), Haemoglobin 13.8 (g/dL), Platelets 155 (×10^9/L), Neutrophils 45 (%), Eosinophils 14 (%), Absolute eosinophil count 0.868 (×10^9/L), Band neutrophils 1 (%), Lymphocytes 36 (%), Monocytes 4 (%), and Basophils 0 (%). The chest radiograph does not show any abnormalities. Serology for filarial infections was positive. Day-blood samples were collected, filtered, and stained with Giemsa, which revealed sheathed microfilariae with a tapered tail characteristic for Loa loa. The microfilarial count was 1400/mL. Prior 24-hour ECG showed paroxysmal supraventricular extrasystoles, and echocardiography showed a minimal pericardial effusion.
differential_diagnosis: Differential diagnoses for skin swellings and eosinophilia include non-specific urticaria, Calabar swellings in loiasis, cysticercosis, larva currens in Strongyloides stercoralis infection, and infection with Mansonella perstans. Acute schistosomiasis was considered, but deemed unlikely due to the patient being afebrile and the migratory swellings not fitting the clinical picture. Gnathostomiasis and sparganosis were also considered, though these infections are more common in East Asia than in Africa.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was treated with caution, first with albendazole followed by ivermectin. Therapy was tolerated well. The absolute eosinophil count (AEC) returned to normal, and the microfilarial count declined. No sequelae were observed, and the palpitations settled. Follow-up echocardiography 3 months later was normal, the pericardial effusion had resolved, and 24-hour ECG was also normal.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is Loiasis, caused by the filarial nematode Loa loa. This diagnosis is supported by the patient's 4-year residency in Cameroon, the presence of transient subcutaneous swellings, eosinophilia, positive serology for filarial infections, and the identification of Loa loa microfilariae in a blood smear with a count of 1400/mL. Her cardiac arrhythmia and pericardial effusion resolved after treatment, though it remains unclear if there was any direct association between the infection and the patient's transient cardiac problems.

tables.title: Full Blood Count Results at Presentation
Treatment of Loiasis Matched to Levels of Microfilaraemia (After Boussinesq 2012)
rows: Albendazole 200mg bd for 21 days, followed by ivermectin 150µg/kg stat, then DEC at slowly increasing doses.
Ivermectin 150 µg/kg stat, repeat after 1-3 months until microfilaraemia is <2000 mf/mL, this is followed by treatment with DEC.

DEC: start with low doses of 3-6 mg/d if there are parasites in the blood, 50 mg/d if amicrofilaraemic, divided into 2-3 doses. The dose is doubled every day up to 400 mg/d, still divided into 2-3 doses. Start treatment in hospital. Oral antihistamines or corticosteroids may be useful during the first days of treatment to reduce side effects (arthralgias, pruritus, headache, fever). Several 3- to 4-week courses of DEC administered at intervals of 2-3 weeks may be required to achieve a complete cure.
